instagram_caption:
🚨 Subscriber Crown: the wild rise and unexpected stalls of YouTube’s biggest channels

From a handful of creators in 2010 to corporate music labels and kids’ channels dominating the platform, YouTube’s top ranks tell a story of scale, spectacle and shifting attention. Remember the 2018–2019 PewDiePie vs T-Series saga? That was the turning point: an indie creator who spent years building a global audience suddenly found himself neck-and-neck with a corporate music behemoth. PewDiePie hit 100M in August 2019 — a landmark moment — but T-Series’ banded growth and India’s internet boom pushed them past 100M the same year and then into the 200M+ club by the mid-2020s.

Kids’ content exploded too. Cocomelon broke 100M in 2020 as young viewers and parents turned to repeatable nursery content; by 2024 it sat north of ~150M. SET India and other regional media channels rode local content scale, moving from single-digit millions in the early 2010s to 100M+ by the early 2020s as India’s streaming base ballooned.

Then a new kind of creator arrived: MrBeast. Jimmy Donaldson turned virality into a machine — elaborate stunts, high-budget giveaways, and consistent churn of hits. He crossed 100M in 2022 and kept growing aggressively, showing creators can still climb to the very top with reinvestment and global appeal.

So what’s the headline? Corporate channels (T-Series, SET India) and kids’ networks (Cocomelon) scaled with distribution and repeatable content, while creators like PewDiePie plateaued after hitting the cultural peak — and a new wave of creators (MrBeast) used spectacle to climb even higher.

Which of these stories surprised you most — the corporate takeover, kids’ content dominance, or MrBeast’s creator superpower? Drop your pick below and tell us why.

Cocomelon’s repeatable children’s content pushed it past 100M in 2020, and creator MrBeast broke the mold by hitting 100M in 2022 and continuing rapid growth.
